statement: In an international online survey of people who had drunk ayahuasca (2017 to 2019; 6,877 self-selected respondents who had drunk with no more than two groups; Perkins et al., 2021), the setting of their last ceremony, as they described and rated it looking back, was associated with how much extreme fear they recalled and with difficulties afterwards, by small amounts. Of the 6,817 with a known setting, 52.1% had last drunk in an ayahuasca church (87% of them living in Brazil, and more than half having drunk over 200 times), 19.6% with traditional shamans and 28.3% in other settings, where most had drunk five times or fewer. Adjusted for age, sex, education, number of mental-health diagnoses, times drunk, years since the last drink and the other setting variables, each point higher on a 1-to-4 rating of support and safety (averages 3.4 to 3.9) went with less extreme fear or panic (−0.29 on a 0-to-10 scale, SE 0.07) and fewer difficulties in the weeks after (−0.13, SE 0.05); each point higher on a rating of the preparation offered (a chance to discuss one's history and concerns, and guidance on difficulties, before drinking) went with fewer later difficulties (−0.14, SE 0.03) but not with less fear (−0.01, p = 0.82). More fear went with more traditional practices (0.18 per practice, of up to 6), with drinking mostly in Amazonian countries other than Brazil (0.7), with therapeutic reasons for drinking (0.21 per reason) and with mental-health diagnoses (0.21 per diagnosis); less fear went with church features such as hymns or sermons (−0.38) and with each decade of age (−0.22). Fasting, offered at 35% of traditional and 26% of other settings, was associated with no difference in fear, later difficulties or current mental health, and with slightly higher ratings of mystical experience (1.7 points on a 9-to-90 scale) and of growth in well-being. Across the whole range of either rating, current distress differed by under 2 points on the 40-point Kessler scale (editors' arithmetic). Ratings and outcomes were reported by the same people at one sitting, on average 1.2 to 1.6 years after their last drink; nothing was measured before ayahuasca, the amount and content of the brew were not recorded, and the authors note that the sample may lean towards people with good experiences. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one large survey, people who felt safe and supported at their last ayahuasca ceremony recalled a little less fear and fewer problems in the weeks after. Being offered a chance to talk things through beforehand went with fewer problems afterwards, but not with less fear, and fasting went with neither. The same people rated the ceremony and their experience, looking back, and the differences were small.
population: People who have drunk ayahuasca, self-selected through ayahuasca organizations, retreat centres, churches and online groups (half of them church members, mostly in Brazil)
exposure: Features of the last ceremony as the respondents described and rated them: church, traditional-shaman or other setting; support and safety; preparation offered; traditional or religious practices; fasting; country where they mostly drank
comparator: Respondents who rated or described their last ceremony differently, adjusted for age, sex, education, mental-health diagnoses, times drunk and years since the last drink
outcome: Extreme fear or panic during a session (0 to 10), difficulties in the weeks or months after, mystical-experience and growth ratings, and current distress (Kessler-10)
magnitude: Adjusted B (SE): support and safety (per point, 1 to 4) extreme fear −0.29 (0.07), later difficulties −0.13 (0.05), Kessler-10 −0.62 (0.12); preparation offered (per point) later difficulties −0.14 (0.03), fear −0.01 (p = 0.82), Kessler-10 −0.25 (0.07); extreme fear: traditional practices 0.18 per practice, traditional country 0.7, therapeutic motivation 0.21, mental-health diagnoses 0.21, church features −0.38, age −0.22 per decade; fasting: no association with fear, later difficulties or mental health, mystical orientation 1.69 (0.64), growth 0.97 (0.37). Across a whole rating, under 2 Kessler-10 points (editors' arithmetic).

statement: In people who use classic psychedelics, feeling safe and supported is associated with fewer reported difficulties in retrospective surveys, while the one prospective study found only a weak, uncertain link for the place and the people. In that study (Haijen et al., 2018; about 198 self-selected adults planning their own experience), a good feeling about the people who would be present and about the place, rated within the day before, went with slightly lower Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores rated about a day after (standardized beta −0.14, p = 0.070, not statistically significant), and a retreat or a setting designed for therapy, reported afterwards as one yes-or-no item, was associated with no acute measure (0.02); the authors note that the term was not defined for participants. In an international online survey of 6,877 self-selected people who had drunk ayahuasca, each point higher on a 1-to-4 rating of support and safety at their last ceremony went with 0.29 points less extreme fear or panic on a 0-to-10 scale (95% CI 0.15 to 0.43, editors' calculation), slightly fewer difficulties in the weeks after, and current distress lower by 0.62 points on the 40-point Kessler scale, under 2 points across the whole rating (editors' arithmetic), after adjustment for age, sex, education, mental-health diagnoses, times drunk and years since the last drink; the ratings were made looking back by the same people, and averaged near the top of the scale (Perkins et al., 2021). Among 613 US adults in an online panel who had used a classic psychedelic, those who blamed a lack of psychological support for their most challenging experience rated it as more challenging (beta 0.25) and more often reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others in the days or weeks after (adjusted odds ratio 2.85, 95% CI 1.27 to 6.42; 41 of the 613 reported any); blaming a disagreeable physical environment went with a smaller difference in challenge (0.09) and none in harm thoughts, and blaming the people around with neither (odds ratio for harm thoughts 0.33, 0.11 to 1.01) (Simonsson et al., 2023). Among 163 experienced people recalling two experiences, mostly at home or at a friend's house, those whose experience was at a party, club or festival (24 first and 12 most recent experiences) had higher average challenge scores than the rest (19 against 17 and 31 against 16 per cent of the maximum), a comparison the authors did not test (Palmer and Maynard, 2022). No study compared settings by design. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: In surveys, people who felt safe and supported during a trip reported a little less fear and fewer difficulties, but they rated both afterwards. The one study that asked people beforehand found only a weak, uncertain link between feeling good about the place and the people and how the trip went, and no difference for retreats or settings designed for therapy. No study put people in different settings on purpose to compare them.
population: People who use classic psychedelics outside laboratories: adults planning their own experience (one prospective study), people who drink ayahuasca (one international survey), a US online panel and a self-selected survey of experienced people
exposure: The place and the people: feelings about the setting rated the day before; a retreat or therapeutic setting; support and safety at an ayahuasca ceremony rated afterwards; lack of support, a disagreeable place or disagreeable company blamed for the most challenging experience; party, club or festival settings
comparator: People who rated the setting less favourably, did not blame it, or used elsewhere, within each study
outcome: Challenging experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire), extreme fear or panic, difficulties in the weeks after, thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others, and current distress (Kessler-10)
magnitude: Haijen et al. (2018): setting component and challenging experience beta −0.14 (p = 0.070); retreat or therapeutic setting 0.02 (p = 0.81). Perkins et al. (2021), per point of a 1-to-4 support-and-safety rating: extreme fear (0 to 10) −0.29 (95% CI −0.43 to −0.15, editors'), integration difficulties −0.13, Kessler-10 −0.62 (under 2 points across the whole rating). Simonsson et al. (2023), attributions of the most challenging experience: no support beta 0.25, harm thoughts or attempts adjusted OR 2.85 (1.27 to 6.42); disagreeable physical environment 0.09, OR 0.88 (0.33 to 2.35); disagreeable social environment not associated, OR 0.33 (0.11 to 1.01). Palmer and Maynard (2022), untested: party settings 19.27 against 16.77 (first) and 31.46 against 16.16 (most recent) per cent of the maximum CEQ score.

risk_of_bias.note: Retrospective ratings or attributions made by the same people at the same sitting as the outcome, in self-selected samples, with little or no adjustment (very high risk: sc_perkins_2021, sc_simonsson_2023, sc_palmer_2022); the prospective study is at high risk (confounding, heavy attrition) and its retreat item was undefined (sc_haijen_2018).

inconsistency.note: The retrospective surveys point one way, but the prospective study found only a non-significant trend for the setting rating and no association for a retreat or therapeutic setting, and blaming the people around was not associated with challenge in the panel survey.

indirectness.note: Worded for the people and settings studied.

imprecision.note: Large surveys; the prospective coefficient's interval includes zero, which the statement says.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down two for risk of bias and one for inconsistency, giving very low (the floor). Status mixed: four independent studies, the three retrospective ones pointing towards fewer difficulties with more support, the one prospective study only a non-significant trend for the setting and nothing for a retreat or therapeutic setting; recall at the same sitting may explain the difference, but no study has shown that it does.
